metadata.name: s3
metadata.overview:
Amazon S3 is an object storage service for storing and retrieving any amount of data from anywhere. Data is kept as objects, each made of content and descriptive metadata, inside named containers in a chosen AWS Region.

The service is designed for high durability and availability, with storage classes suited to frequently accessed, infrequently accessed, and archival data. Lifecycle rules, versioning, replication, and write-once-read-many retention help organizations optimize storage over time, recover from mistakes, and meet regulatory requirements.

Stored data is private by default. Access is controlled through identity and resource-based policies and account-wide public access blocking. Encryption at rest and in transit, private network connectivity, and detailed activity logging help protect and audit data. These capabilities help teams build data lakes, host static websites, back up workloads, and feed analytics and machine learning pipelines.
useCases: Building a centralized data lake that holds structured and unstructured data for analytics engines, business intelligence dashboards, and machine learning training pipelines.

Protecting critical data with backups, archives, and disaster recovery copies using versioning, cross-Region replication, and write-once-read-many retention to defend against accidental deletion, ransomware, and regulatory record-keeping gaps.
Hosting static website assets, software downloads, and media libraries, typically served through a content delivery network so the underlying storage stays private.
Centralizing application logs and security audit trails from many accounts into durable, tamper-resistant storage for investigations and compliance reporting.
Running latency-sensitive workloads such as model training or interactive analytics on single-zone high-performance storage co-located with compute resources.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Encryption dependency: SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS use KMS envelope encryption (GenerateDataKey/Decrypt). S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS calls. S3 calls KMS on the requester's behalf via forward access sessions. Directory buckets and UpdateObjectEncryption also depend on KMS.

Access control: identity-based policies, bucket and access point policy evaluation, S3 condition keys, service roles passed via iam:PassRole (replication, Batch Operations, metadata annotation tables), and the Storage Lens service-linked role.
Requests can be signed with STS temporary credentials. S3 Access Grants vends STS credentials to grantees. Presigned URL lifetime is capped by the STS session.

Audit logging: S3 bucket-level calls are recorded as management events by default; object-level data events (AWS::S3::Object, AWS::S3Express::Object, access points) must be enabled. CloudTrail trails also deliver their logs into S3 buckets.
Monitoring: daily storage metrics, request metrics via bucket metrics configurations, replication metrics, Storage Lens metric publishing, and CloudWatch alarms.
Server access logs can be delivered to CloudWatch Logs log groups (with KMS encryption and cross-account aggregation). CloudTrail can also stream S3 API activity to CloudWatch Logs.
Server access logs delivered through CloudWatch Logs can be routed onward to Amazon Data Firehose, including cross-account and cross-Region.
Event notification destination. The topic policy must allow the s3.amazonaws.com principal, ideally scoped with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount.
Event notification destination (standard queues; FIFO queues only through EventBridge). The queue policy must allow the s3.amazonaws.com principal.
Event notification destination, Batch Operations 'Invoke AWS Lambda function' target, and compute behind S3 Object Lambda (WriteGetObjectResponse).
Bucket events can go to Amazon EventBridge for routing (including to SQS FIFO). Also used to track Batch Operations jobs.

Organization-level S3 Block Public Access policies, SCPs and RCPs that constrain S3 access (including root-principal bucket-policy actions), Storage Lens trusted access and delegated admin, and cross-account KMS use within an organization for UpdateObjectEncryption.
GuardDuty S3 Protection analyzes CloudTrail management and data events for S3 to detect exfiltration, destruction, and other suspicious access.
Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data (PII, financial, credentials) in S3 objects and evaluates bucket security posture.
Security Hub CSPM runs S3 controls (e.g., S3.8 Block Public Access) and aggregates findings about S3 resources.
Amazon Detective builds behavior graphs from CloudTrail and GuardDuty findings to investigate activity affecting S3 buckets and objects.
IAM Access Analyzer for S3 flags public and cross-account access granted through bucket policies, ACLs, access point policies, and Multi-Region Access Point policies.

AWS Config records S3 resource configurations (AWS::S3::Bucket and others) and evaluates managed rules such as s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only, and s3-bucket-versioning-enabled.
Trusted Advisor checks S3 buckets for open access permissions, logging configuration, and versioning.
CloudFront serves private S3 origins through origin access control (recommended for static websites and required for SSE-KMS content). Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations.
AWS Backup provides policy-based continuous and periodic S3 backups (versioning required) and backup access points for reading recovery points.

VPC gateway endpoints and PrivateLink interface endpoints provide private connectivity; aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce conditions restrict buckets to specific VPCs or endpoints. EC2 workloads reach S3 using IAM roles.
On-premises networks can reach S3 interface VPC endpoints over AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
Multi-Region Access Points route requests over the AWS global network using AWS Global Accelerator.
S3 Access Grants associates with an IAM Identity Center instance so corporate directory users and groups can be granted access (trusted identity propagation).

Companion control-plane API for access points (including VPC-restricted and Object Lambda), Multi-Region Access Points, Batch Operations jobs, Storage Lens, Access Grants, account-level Block Public Access, and TagResource/UntagResource for ABAC-enabled buckets.

S3 Metadata stores journal, live inventory, and annotation tables in AWS-managed S3 table buckets, so creating a metadata configuration requires s3tables permissions. Table buckets are a sibling S3 bucket type with their own API.
Vector buckets are a sibling S3 bucket type for storing and querying vector embeddings, managed through a dedicated API.
S3 Files provides a shared file system linked to an S3 bucket or prefix, keeping file system and bucket in sync for compute mounts.
S3 on Outposts buckets are created through a separate CreateBucket API; Outposts object data events are logged as AWS::S3Outposts::Object.
Queries S3 data, S3 Inventory reports, server access logs, and S3 Metadata tables.
The AWS Glue Data Catalog and Iceberg REST endpoint make S3 Metadata tables discoverable to analytics services.
Lake Formation governs access to table data, including metadata tables integrated with SageMaker Lakehouse.
Amazon Redshift can query S3 Metadata tables and S3-resident data.
Amazon EMR processes large datasets stored in S3 and can query S3 Metadata tables.
Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse integration makes S3 Metadata and table data queryable by AWS analytics services.
Amazon Quick (QuickSight) can build dashboards over S3 Metadata table query results.
AWS Amplify Hosting is recommended for deploying static website content stored in S3 behind a managed HTTPS CDN.
AWS Transfer Family provides SFTP, FTPS, and FTP transfers into and out of S3.
S3 access points can attach to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS volumes, which use SSE-FSX encryption.
S3 Files is built on Amazon EFS to offer file system semantics over S3 data.
AWS X-Ray traces S3 requests and passes tracing headers to event notification subscribers.
Route 53 provides custom-domain DNS routing for S3 static websites, often together with CloudFront.
AWS-built S3 Object Lambda functions use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII in retrieved objects.
API Gateway is a documented alternative to S3 Object Lambda for invoking Lambda data transformations in front of S3.
AWS Resource Groups (and Tag Editor) help identify and audit security-sensitive S3 resources.
Amazon S3 File Gateway provides on-premises file access to S3 data; object annotations aren't supported through it.

entities.name: AccessPointObject
entities.overview:
An access point object is an Amazon S3 object that applications read, write, and manage through a named S3 access point. Requests target the access point instead of the bucket, while the data remains in its underlying data source, such as a general purpose bucket.

Each request is evaluated against the access point's own policy, network origin, and Block Public Access settings, together with the underlying bucket's permissions. This helps teams give each application or user group a dedicated, narrowly scoped path to shared datasets.

Through an access point, you can upload, download, and delete objects and manage their tags and access control lists. You can also apply Object Lock retention and legal holds, restore archived data, and update encryption settings. Access points accept only HTTPS requests and can be limited to traffic from a specific virtual private cloud.

entities.name: Bucket
entities.overview:
An Amazon S3 bucket is a container that stores objects, such as files and their metadata, in a chosen AWS Region. It is designed to provide durable, scalable storage for data lakes, websites, backups, archives, and application data, with no servers to manage.

Each bucket carries its own settings that shape how its data is protected and used. You can control access with policies and public access blocking, set default encryption, keep multiple object versions, and apply write-once retention rules. Buckets can also replicate data, manage object lifecycles, log requests, and publish event notifications.

Buckets can store data across multiple Availability Zones in a Region, or in a single zone for low-latency or data-residency workloads. Access is private by default, and the owning account controls who can read or write its contents.

entities.name: MultipartUpload
entities.overview:
A multipart upload lets you send a single large object to Amazon S3 as a series of independent parts. Each part is a contiguous portion of the object's data, and parts can be sent in any order or in parallel.

Splitting an upload into parts helps improve throughput and recover quickly from network interruptions. Only failed parts need to be resent, and uploads can be paused and resumed over time. You can also start uploading before the final size is known, or build an object from byte ranges of existing objects.

When all parts are uploaded, Amazon S3 assembles them in part-number order into a single object. Uploaded parts remain stored in the bucket until the upload is completed or stopped. Lifecycle rules can help clean up uploads that are never finished.

entities.name: Object
entities.overview:
An Amazon S3 object is the fundamental unit of data stored in Amazon S3. Each object pairs its content with a unique key, descriptive metadata, and an optional version identifier. Objects reside within buckets and can hold anything from an empty file to multi-terabyte datasets.

You can organize and enrich objects with tags, custom metadata, and larger annotation payloads. Storage classes let you match each object to its access pattern, including archival tiers that require a restore before reading.

Objects are private by default and encrypted at rest automatically. Access is governed through identity and resource policies, time-limited signed URLs, and legacy access control lists. Versioning, retention settings, and legal holds help protect objects from accidental or malicious overwrites and deletions, while checksums help verify integrity.

entities.name: ObjectLambdaAccessPoint
entities.overview:
An Object Lambda access point is an Amazon S3 endpoint that runs your AWS Lambda code on data as it is retrieved. Read, list, and metadata requests sent through the endpoint invoke the attached function, and the transformed result returns to the application. Other requests are handled as standard S3 requests without transformation.

The endpoint reads source data through a designated standard S3 access point, known as the supporting access point. Typical uses include redacting sensitive fields, filtering rows, resizing or watermarking images, decompressing files, and customizing object listings or metadata. This helps you serve different views of shared data without storing derivative copies, running proxies, or changing application code.

The endpoint is designed to serve only authenticated callers and does not permit anonymous access. You govern its use with an optional resource policy, together with permissions for the caller, the supporting access point, and the function.

mitigations.statement: Amazon S3 service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon S3 API calls from your VPCs can target buckets in another account. Restricting those calls to resources in your organization enforces the resource perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon S3 service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: Amazon S3 API calls from your VPCs can be made by identities outside your organization. Restricting those calls to principals in your organization enforces the identity perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon S3 access point object resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an access point in another account can grant your principals read, write, and delete access to objects through it. That access also requires permission from the access point's bucket or other data source and from your identity-based policies. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to trusted resources, such as those your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 access point object should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: `PutObject` and `UpdateObjectEncryption` calls through an access point can set an access point object's encryption to SSE-KMS under a customer managed key. Using a customer managed key gives you full control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 access point object should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 access point object supports an object access control list (ACL) that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. When the bucket's S3 Object Ownership setting enables ACLs, requests through an access point can name other AWS accounts as grantees. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your access point objects to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 access point object should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an access point object at upload through `$.x-amz-tagging`, a URL-encoded set of key/value pairs, or later by calling `PutObjectTagging`, independently of the access point's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each access point object supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's replication role and annotation table role should be assumed only by Amazon S3 acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You can pass a replication role through your bucket's `$.ReplicationConfiguration.Role` setting and an annotation table role through its `$.MetadataConfiguration.AnnotationTableConfiguration.Role` setting, and each role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon S3, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume those roles helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming them.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should have S3 Inventory and S3 Storage Class Analysis enabled to collect detailed non-CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon S3 bucket supports S3 Inventory through inventory configurations, and general purpose buckets also support S3 Storage Class Analysis through analytics configurations. These features capture detailed operational and security telemetry, such as per-object encryption status and access patterns by object age group, kept outside Amazon CloudWatch Metrics.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Requests to your bucket can originate from public IP addresses or from VPCs through VPC endpoints, and the bucket policy specifies who can make them and under which conditions. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your bucket can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon S3 bucket resources

mitigationContext.context: A bucket policy on a bucket in another account can grant your principals permission to call its bucket-level operations, such as `HeadBucket` or `CreateSession`. When that bucket is a replication destination, its bucket policy can also grant your replication role permission to replicate objects into it. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be protected by an AWS Backup backup plan

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket stores your objects and their versions, tags, ACLs, and user-defined metadata. AWS Backup supports the bucket as an independently protectable resource type and captures its contents in periodic or continuous recovery points.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be deployed across more than one Availability Zone with the general purpose bucket type

mitigationContext.context: The general purpose bucket type, selected at creation unless `$.CreateBucketConfiguration.Bucket.Type` is set to `Directory`, stores objects across at least three Availability Zones, except in S3 One Zone-IA. Deploying an Amazon S3 bucket across more than one Availability Zone helps keep it and its data available when one Availability Zone fails.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket and its metadata journal table, metadata live inventory table, metadata annotation table, inventory report, and replica object should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Default encryption with SSE-KMS can encrypt new objects written to your bucket under a customer managed key that you specify. Your bucket's S3 Metadata tables, S3 Inventory reports, and replica objects can each use a separately configured customer managed key. Using customer managed keys gives you full control over key lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket can carry its own bucket policy that names the IAM principals allowed to access the bucket and objects, set through `$.Policy`. Requiring explicit principal definitions rather than wildcard principals helps prevent the bucket from inadvertently being made public or accessible to unintended actors.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should replicate objects to at least one other AWS Region

mitigationContext.context: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) uses your general purpose bucket's replication configuration to copy new and updated objects to destination buckets in other AWS Regions. Automated replication of that data to a different AWS Region supports multi-Region resiliency.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's inventory configuration and event notification configuration should only be configured with a trusted S3 bucket, SNS topic, SQS queue, or Lambda function

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket's inventory configuration and event notification configuration set their destinations through `$.InventoryConfiguration.Destination.S3BucketDestination.Bucket`, `$.NotificationConfiguration.TopicConfiguration[*].Topic`, `$.NotificationConfiguration.QueueConfiguration[*].Queue`, and `$.NotificationConfiguration.CloudFunctionConfiguration[*].CloudFunction`, which can name S3 buckets, SNS topics, SQS queues, or Lambda functions in another account. Restricting the destinations helps keep your inventory reports and event notifications flowing only to trusted targets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket supports a resource-based policy, called a bucket policy, that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your buckets and their objects to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be accessed by an AWS service principal, such as the AWS CloudTrail service principal, only when the service principal is acting on behalf of a trusted resource, AWS account, or organization

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on your bucket can grant an AWS service principal, such as the AWS CloudTrail service principal (`cloudtrail.amazonaws.com`), access to the bucket and its objects. That policy should restrict which accounts or resources the service may act on behalf of.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be governed by a policy that requires all connections to be encrypted in transit

mitigationContext.context: Amazon S3 supports resource-based bucket policies. Amazon S3 accepts requests to your general purpose bucket over unencrypted HTTP connections by default, while directory bucket endpoints are HTTPS only; a resource-based policy can require encryption in transit, as a defense-in-depth measure on directory buckets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be protected by Amazon S3 Block Public Access

mitigationContext.context: Amazon S3 Block Public Access settings override public access that bucket policies and access control lists (ACLs) can grant to your bucket and its objects. They are configurable on general purpose buckets and permanently enabled on directory buckets. These dedicated settings give you a centralized toggle that helps prevent public access without requiring additional network or IAM controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a bucket at creation through the `$.CreateBucketConfiguration.Tags[*].Key` and `$.CreateBucketConfiguration.Tags[*].Value` request parameters, a list of key-value pairs, and afterward through `PutBucketTagging` or S3 Control `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each bucket supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should encrypt new objects by default with a customer managed KMS key

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket carries the default KMS key for objects written to it. Once set, that default applies a customer managed key to new objects created without an explicit key.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should be configured to disallow bucket policy modifications that would remove all policy-management access for the bucket

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon S3 bucket carries a resource-based policy, known as a bucket policy, that governs `s3:PutBucketPolicy` and `s3:DeleteBucketPolicy` for general purpose buckets. A policy write that removes all policy-management access can leave the bucket unmanageable and its stored data inaccessible.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket should have request metrics and S3 Replication metrics enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Your bucket can enable request metrics through the `$.MetricsConfiguration` metrics configuration and S3 Replication metrics through the `$.ReplicationConfiguration.Rule[*].Destination.Metrics.Status` metrics status of each replication rule, adding minute-by-minute CloudWatch metrics beyond the default daily storage metrics. Collecting those metrics improves security visibility by providing finer-grained data for anomaly detection and incident response.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to performing multipart uploads on trusted Amazon S3 buckets

mitigationContext.context: A bucket policy or access control list (ACL) on a bucket in another account can grant your principals multipart upload access. Your multipart upload calls act on the bucket, access point, or copy-source object that each request names. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 object's multipart upload should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: The `$.x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id` request parameter on `CreateMultipartUpload` specifies the AWS KMS key that encrypts your object's multipart upload's parts and the object assembled from them. Using a customer managed key for this encryption gives you full control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon S3 bucket's object resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy or access control list on an Amazon S3 bucket in another account can grant your principals access to its objects. Your principals can then call object operations such as `GetObject`, `PutObject`, and `CopyObject` on that bucket, directly or through an access point. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's object should be deployed across more than one Availability Zone with the S3 storage class

mitigationContext.context: The S3 storage class you set through the `$.x-amz-storage-class` request parameter of `PutObject` or `CopyObject` determines whether your object's data is stored redundantly across a minimum of three Availability Zones or, for S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Express One Zone, in only one. Deploying an Amazon S3 bucket's object across more than one Availability Zone helps keep it and its data available when one Availability Zone fails.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's object should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) encrypts your bucket's object's data at rest under a KMS key that your write request can specify. When a write request omits encryption settings, your bucket's default encryption configuration supplies the encryption type and key. Encrypting your bucket's object with a customer managed key gives you full control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's object should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon S3 bucket's object, when the bucket has access control lists (ACLs) enabled, supports an object ACL that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your objects to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket's object should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an object through the `$.x-amz-tagging` list of key/value pairs on upload or copy, or later through `PutObjectTagging`, separately from its bucket's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each bucket's object supports.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon S3 object lambda access point resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Object Lambda Access Point in another account can grant your principals `s3-object-lambda:GetObject` and other S3 Object Lambda permissions. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon S3 service API calls

threatContext.context: Amazon S3 is reachable from your VPC through a gateway VPC endpoint or an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). An IAM principal from outside your organization can use that network path to make Amazon S3 API calls with its own credentials. That access enables transfer of data from your VPC to Amazon S3 buckets in an AWS account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon S3 resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: Amazon S3 API calls from your VPCs can target buckets in another account. An IAM principal on your network whose credentials hold permissions on such a bucket can copy your data into it or download untrusted content from it.
`GetObject` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`GetObjectVersion` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`HeadBucket` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`ListBucket` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`PutObject` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`PutObjectAcl` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon S3 access point object
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the object data and object versions it writes or updates through the access point with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to write an access point object or update its encryption chooses the KMS key that encrypts your object data by setting `$.x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id` and `$.ObjectEncryption.SSEKMS.KMSKeyArn`. If that key material sits outside your control, its holder can later revoke or delete it and leave that object data unreadable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon S3 access point object
threats.threatAction: can configure the access point object without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon S3 access point object can omit the required tags, for example by uploading the object without `$.x-amz-tagging`. An access point object left without those tags may fall outside ownership attribution and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon S3 access point object
threats.threatAction: can encrypt its data with an AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to create or modify your Amazon S3 access point object chooses whether the AWS managed key protects its data at rest. You cannot govern that key's policy or lifecycle.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon S3 access point object
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted access point object, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: An Amazon S3 access point object in an account outside your organization can grant your principals access through access point policies, bucket policies, and object ACLs. Your principals can then name its access point in `$.Bucket` and call `PutObject` or `UploadPartCopy` to send your data, or `GetObject` to receive data. They can also call `UploadPartCopy` with that access point object in `$.x-amz-copy-source` to copy its data into your multipart upload in the same Region.
`GetObject` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`PutObject` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.
`PutObjectAcl` might require access to service-owned buckets, which are buckets that are managed in service accounts.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read object data from an Amazon S3 access point object that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext object data in the access point object

threatContext.context: Without a customer managed key, your access point object's data is encrypted under Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) or the AWS managed key `aws/s3`, neither of which you can disable or restrict through your own key policy. An IAM principal holding the permission to call `GetObject` or `SelectObjectContent` through your access point can read that data in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon S3 access point object through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my access point object

threatContext.context: The resource-based policy on your Amazon S3 access point can grant object read, write, or delete access to principals outside your organization, and requests through the access point can set the object's access control list (ACL) to grant other AWS accounts access when the bucket's S3 Object Ownership setting enables ACLs. When the underlying bucket also permits the request, such a principal can call `GetObject` with its own credentials to read your access point object. With write or delete access, it can overwrite the object by calling `PutObject` or delete it by calling `DeleteObject`.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read object data from an Amazon S3 access point object that is encrypted with an AWS managed KMS key in the same account as the principal
threats.threatAction: can read the object data in the access point object

threatContext.context: Your Amazon S3 access point object can be encrypted with the AWS managed key `aws/s3`, whose key policy AWS establishes and you do not manage and which admits every same-account principal using the key through the service. A same-account IAM principal with unintended read permissions on the access point object, such as `s3:GetObject` or `s3:GetObjectVersion`, receives the object's data in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify a bucket policy governing an Amazon S3 bucket
threats.threatAction: can make the bucket inaccessible by modifying the bucket resource-based policy

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your bucket policy (`s3:PutBucketPolicy`) can replace that policy with one that denies policy-management and object access actions to all principals. The bucket remains in place but unmanageable by every IAM user and role, because the policy also denies them later changes to itself, leaving its stored objects unreachable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to configure my Amazon S3 bucket's inventory configuration and event notification configuration
threats.threatAction: can configure my S3 bucket to use an untrusted S3 bucket, SNS topic, SQS queue, or Lambda function to deliver inventory reports and event notifications

threatContext.context: An IAM principal that creates or modifies your Amazon S3 bucket can set its inventory or event notification destination to a resource outside your organization. Amazon S3 can then deliver your inventory reports and event notifications to that resource once its owner grants Amazon S3 access.

`PutBucketInventoryConfiguration` allows you to specify an S3 bucket that does not belong to your organization as the value for the `Destination` request parameter. Because the subsequent call against the S3 bucket is performed by the service principal, it is not restricted with `aws:ResourceOrgID` implemented in a service control policy.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if the S3 buckets are encrypted with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
managedImplementation.description: Checks if the S3 buckets are encrypted with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if the S3 bucket is not encrypted with an AWS KMS key.

managedImplementation.title: Require an Amazon S3 bucket to have server-side encryption configured using an AWS KMS key
managedImplementation.description: This control checks whether default server-side encryption is enabled on an Amazon S3 bucket using AWS KMS.

managedImplementation.title: Disallow public read access to S3 buckets
managedImplementation.description: Secure access to data stored in Amazon S3 buckets by disallowing public reads.

managedImplementation.title: Require an Amazon S3 bucket to have block public access settings configured
managedImplementation.description: This control checks whether your Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket has a bucket-level Block Public Access (BPA) configuration.

managedImplementation.title: Disallow public write access to S3 buckets
managedImplementation.description: Secure access to data stored in Amazon S3 buckets by disallowing public writes.

managedImplementation.title: Disallow public read access to log archive
managedImplementation.description: Control access to your log archive's Amazon S3 bucket by disallowing public read access.

managedImplementation.title: Disallow public write access to log archive
managedImplementation.description: Control access to your log archive's Amazon S3 bucket by disallowing public write access.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if S3 buckets have replication rules enabled
managedImplementation.description: Checks if S3 buckets have replication rules enabled. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if an S3 bucket does not have a replication rule or has a replication rule that is not enabled.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if you have enabled S3 Cross-Region Replication for your Amazon S3 buckets
managedImplementation.description: Checks if you have enabled S3 Cross-Region Replication for your Amazon S3 buckets. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if there are no replication rules enabled for Cross-Region Replication.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon S3 Events Notifications are enabled on an S3 bucket
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon S3 Events Notifications are enabled on an S3 bucket. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if S3 Events Notifications are not set on a bucket, or if the event type or destination do not match the eventTypes and destinationArn parameters.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if S3 buckets are publicly accessible
managedImplementation.description: Checks if S3 buckets are publicly accessible. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if an S3 bucket is not listed in the excludedPublicBuckets parameter and bucket level settings are public.

managedImplementation.title: Require that an Amazon S3 bucket does not manage user access with an access control list (ACL)
managedImplementation.description: This control checks whether your Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket allows user permissions through access control lists.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Buckets allow user permissions through access control lists (ACLs)
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Buckets allow user permissions through access control lists (ACLs). The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if ACLs are configured for user access in Amazon S3 Buckets.

managedImplementation.title: Require that Amazon S3 bucket requests use Secure Sockets Layer
managedImplementation.description: This control checks whether Amazon S3 bucket policies require requests to use Secure Socket Layer (SSL).

managedImplementation.title: Checks if S3 buckets have policies that require requests to use SSL/TLS
managedImplementation.description: Checks if S3 buckets have policies that require requests to use SSL/TLS. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if any S3 bucket has policies allowing HTTP requests.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon S3 buckets have tags
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon S3 buckets have tags. Optionally, you can specify tag keys. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if there are no tags or if the specified tag keys are not present. The rule does not check for tags starting with 'aws:'.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if S3 buckets are publicly accessible
managedImplementation.description: Checks if S3 buckets are publicly accessible. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if an S3 bucket is not listed in the excludedPublicBuckets parameter and bucket level settings are public.
